title: Remembering Les Kaye
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The talk highlights the importance of community and connection in Zen practice, drawing from personal experiences with Les Kaye, who introduced Nomon Tim Burnett to Soto Zen at age 18. Nomon reflects on how this experience shaped their understanding of the value of community and connection in deepening one's practice. This is contrasted with Suzuki Roshi's approach to teaching, which emphasized direct experience and immersion over intellectual understanding, trusting that students would learn through action and observation rather than explanation.

sentences.text: Thank you for being here, and thank you especially for your willingness to try to figure all this choreography out.
Some of it is just common sense.
I appreciate it.
You two guys were like, "Hey, we're way back here.
We could move forward.
That would be better."
Some of it is just common sense, but you don't know what the context is, right?
So you're a little bit running blind.
Of course, part of the Zen design is that it's so beautiful to be together quietly and harmoniously.
We're trying to do these fairly intricate procedures and dances without talking.
It gets a little bit complicated, but we're figuring it out.
Thank you for your willingness to dance with it.
It may be slightly easier when there are more people around you, more familiar.
You can follow along, but that can be hazardous, too, because somebody may look very confident and be doing it not the way that we want to do it.
So we try to be relaxed about it, but it is so beautiful when it all clicks.
It's really beautiful, don't you think?
People moving together.

We sometimes say it's like one body moving through the meditations and the walking and the cleaning and studying the Dharma together in the talk, like one integrated being, which is what we actually are.
We just think otherwise, right?
We think we're probably separate.
So that's one of the purposes of all the intricate formalities and forms.
It's just another way for us to unwind a little bit our sense of separation and distinctness.
We're all in it together.
We know that.
That was one of the few good things about the pandemic, I thought: that phrase was used so strongly.
We're in this together.
Anyway, I want to talk about something else.

A little bit of my history, and then a little bit of a profile and an appreciation for one of our Americans and teachers who helped to bring this way of being, this choreography, to America, to the West.
So in the spring of 1984, I was 18 years old.
I was a high school senior enrolled in an alternative program called the Learning Community.
I could say a lot about that year.
I learned so much.
Integrated, multidisciplinary, self-organized: you had to organize yourself and take responsibility.
The teacher was very good at seeing into these teenagers' souls and just giving them little nudges, like a Zen master himself.
So I learned a lot about how to be a person and how to be with others in this program, after the previous however many years cranking away, doing my homework and stuff.
There's a lot less homework and a lot more interpersonal learning in the Learning Community.
We also did learn content, and the teacher and founder of this wanted us, middle class teenagers, to have a little more of a clue about the diversity of cultures and spirituality.
So he created a course that he called Eastern Psychology, which was partly to dodge the school board a little bit, because you're not supposed to do religion in a public high school.
And it wasn't just reading about it.

Most comparative religion classes (I visited comparative religion classes in high schools in Whatcom County, actually) read about it, and maybe they invite somebody to come to the classroom, but they don't actually go and do it.
In our case, we went and did it.
It was a pretty small class, so it just took a couple of parent helpers to drive us around.
We went to ashrams and mosques and yoga studios.
And we went to a little Zen Buddhist center.
The Zen Buddhist center was a converted, quite small church.
I guess it had been a Pentecostal church, I learned recently.
I lived in Palo Alto, California, and the high school was in Los Altos, and this was in Mountain View, those places named after you.
All these areas are now the hub of Silicon Valley, and you can't buy a shack for under two million, but this was before all that, before Silicon Valley sprung forth.
Just ordinary California suburban towns, with different spaces where people were doing pretty unique things, including this little place called Kanondo.
It means a compassion way, compassion place, the way of compassion.
We actually got there somehow a little before our host, probably because he was running home on a lunch break from work.
So we were just hanging around outside this little Zen center in the gardens.
Then we heard an odd whack, whack, whack, whack, whack, whack, whack, whack, whack, whack sound, which we kind of ignored.
What was that?
A strange woodpecker or something.
And then this guy, maybe about the age I am now, or a little younger (forties, fifties, maybe would have been a little younger), appeared out of nowhere in black robes and gestured to us.
He didn't even talk to us.
He just gestured to us.
Somehow I got the impression that we were supposed to have done something, from the whacking sound, that we didn't know about.
Of course, that was the same whacker we have out here called the Han.
This teacher, this priest, told us a few things.
He gave us, I think, the very basics of how to enter the room, right, like there is here.
And we went inside.
I don't remember what he said, but we went inside.
It was the space that really impressed me.
It was a little bit dim, like here.
It was very orderly, everything lined up, very clean, dark wood.
There was some kind of mysterious lighting, like the altar, candles lit and stuff like that, statues, which I didn't know what they were, flowers.
But it wasn't the details that impressed me.
It was something just about the vibe of the space.
It just felt so, I don't know what to call this space.
Looking back, maybe I'd say grounded, peaceful, but stronger than peaceful: settled, a very settled space.
I remember thinking, well, this space is very neat and clean.
But my mom was a bit obsessed with neat and clean, and I didn't appreciate that very much as a teenager.
So it wasn't that exactly.
It was somehow a different kind of neat and clean.
Of course, when you're a teenager, maybe it's just that it's not your mom making it that makes it better anyway.
I don't know.
Sorry, mom.
But something really impressed me about this space that's really stuck in me.
I'm pretty sure I remember him showing us the basics of how to do meditation.
We sat for not too long, 15 or 20 minutes.
He knew who he was dealing with.
And maybe he didn't have much time himself.
I think afterwards he gave a few words or told a little story or something.
I don't remember any of that.
But I remember the space.
Somehow seeing that space when I was 18 changed my life in a radical way.
And here we are, however many years later; it would be 42.
The math says that.
So what I want to talk about is that man that I don't remember much about from then.
I got to know him a little bit later.
That priest was a man named Les Kaye, and I bring him up because he just passed away.
Over the years, getting more into this Zen thing, I would go back and visit Kanondo, visit Les Kaye.
Usually when I was back down in California, we had moved away, visiting my mom.
I'd slip away one morning, one of those sort of drifty mornings of family visiting, with all that like, "What are we going to do today?
Who's coming?
What's up with cousin so-and-so, blah, blah, blah, blah."
I'd slip away early in the morning.
I think sometimes I didn't even tell them.
Actually, one time I remember I borrowed the car without asking at six, five in the morning, and I got scolded.
We got up and the car was gone.
They freaked out: was it stolen?
So I slipped down there and I practiced with Les Kaye at Kanondo.
He was one of these really solid people.
Not so flashy.
He was learned, but not like an incredible scholar or anything.
He was really in his body.
He really loved the practice and he really loved being with people practicing.
He came just after the very first wave of people who gathered around the Japanese teacher Suzuki Roshi in the sixties.
He appeared on the scene later in the sixties.
Unlike many of his fellow students, he was a little bit older, but he also had a very different orientation.

Many of his fellows and students were college dropouts, really looking for an alternative lifestyle and an alternative to this dominant society, many of whom really saw Zen as a way to subvert or change or reinvent all of society.
But actually Les was not so much like that.
He had an engineering degree and he had gotten a salaried job at IBM.
So this was before Silicon Valley: an engineer, a computer engineer.
There weren't that many of them then.
And he had been in the Army, in the military as well, which was unusual for the early students.
But he had this feeling, like so many of us do, that there's something missing here.
"I have a great life."
He married young.
I think the marriage lasted until she died many, many years later, and then he passed.
"I've got a good life, I've got a good job, but something isn't quite something.
Something's missing."

I forget exactly; somebody gave him a book on Buddhism, or he ran into something about Buddhism, and heard on the grapevine, [unclear: "most"] had friends who were more like hippies, about this Zen master in San Francisco.
So he went to see him and was deeply impressed.
Let me read you a little bit about that first meeting.
Not too long ago, a couple of years ago, some of his students worked together to create a book of this teacher's talks and teachings.
He wrote a book or two as well, but this was created by his students.
*Suzuki Roshi described how we get lost when we're caught up in the excitement and the overwhelming busyness of everyday life.
In 1969, a year before his book, Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind was published, I experienced this truth face to face.
In the fall of that year, still very near to Zen practice, he started at a little group in Los Altos,* actually.
*I attended a ceremony at the San Francisco Zen Center, followed by an informal lunch where we all sat at long tables in the dining room.
And I happened to be across from Suzuki Roshi.
I felt a rush of anticipation and excitement.
I have so many questions, I thought.
Here is a chance to ask them.*
*But not wanting to seem anxious or intrusive, I waited for eye contact to occur by chance, for Suzuki Roshi to engage with me, to ask me how I was, to start a conversation.
But Suzuki Roshi never looked up.
His eyes remained on his food.
Remaining silent too, I observed how attentively he picked up his bowl, how he embraced the simple meal with such care.
My eagerness to ask questions went into remission.* Like a disease.
I like that word, remission.
*My eagerness to ask questions went into remission.
My compulsion to speak evaporated.
My desire to know, know, know drifted away.
I kept my awareness on the mindful way that he handled his utensils and bowls, and by contrast, how I handled mine.
The quiet meal ended with the sound of two clappers,* two wooden sticks hit together as in a Zen monastery, *with a short chant.
We bowed.
As we bowed, our eyes met across the table.
We did greet each other, speak for a few moments and parts, but I no longer felt the need to ask my question.
From that time on, I just wanted to live with that simplicity and ease, not caught in eagerness for stimulation and attention.*
That was his first encounter with Suzuki Roshi in 1969 at the pretty much brand new San Francisco Zen Center.
They'd moved there the year before.

So he kept going to the little sitting group in a converted garage in Los Altos, and Suzuki Roshi would come there from time to time and give little talks, which actually were the little talks that became the book, Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind.
And he kept practicing.
He kept studying.

A little while later, Suzuki Roshi, who was getting pretty busy with the big center in San Francisco and their monastery by Big Sur, invited another priest to be the teacher down at that end of the San Francisco Bay Peninsula, named Kobun Chino Otogawa.
So he didn't see Suzuki Roshi quite as much.
And here our histories converge a bit, Red Cedar's and theirs, I mean, because about a year later along came another student named Edie Norton, who was a longtime member here who since passed.
So she knew Les pretty well.
And she really loved Kobun Chino.
By the way, just yesterday I put a picture of Kobun Chino up on the ancestors altar space on the wall there, so we can remember him.
I never met Koban, but by all accounts, a wonderful guy and an exasperating guy.
He was always off somewhere else when you needed him.
But pretty much that meant you had to figure it out yourself.
It turned out to be good, that kind of teacher.
But Les was not that kind of teacher.
He was a here-every-day, every-morning, every-week, every-year kind of teacher.
I didn't visit Kanondo that many times, but maybe a dozen times over 20 years, and there was never a time that he wasn't there.
And I doubt there were many times that he wasn't there when I wasn't there either.
The practice was simple and quiet.
I'm sure at times Les Kaye gave Dharma talks and had Dokusan meetings with the students and did all the different things that you have to do to take care of a Sangha and be a teacher.
But his main activity was Zazen and a simple service with the Sangha.
And then coffee.
There always was coffee after sitting in the morning.
He really liked coffee.
Maybe that's how I got the bug.
But at the coffees, he would never, well, he'd ask me to remind him who he was, but he wouldn't ask me lots of questions or do any probing or anything like that.
I've known other teachers that you end up in one-on-one with, and they're asking you what your deepest concern is and what your purpose in life is.
I had a major encounter like that this last spring.
I was like, "Oh my gosh, I thought we were having pizza.
We're having Dokusan."
That was a different teacher.
But Les wasn't like that.
He'd always have a quiet smile.
You can just tell he's just enjoying being with people who practiced.
And that was pretty much his whole life.
Eventually the Sangha outgrew the little converted Pentecostal church, which was on, I almost remember the name of the street.
It might have been called Church Street, actually.
They managed to buy property and build a Zendo from the ground up.
By then, in 2006, it was Silicon Valley, and property cost a lot of money, as did building.
So it's amazing they pulled it off.
Their Sangha is not that much bigger than Red Cedar.
A bit bigger, I'm sure, but not that much.
Then Les did go on to ask Suzuki Roshi to please ordain him as a priest, as a monk.
So here's his memory of that.
The little book they put together of his talks is called I Had a Good Teacher.
It's referring to Suzuki Roshi.
And this is the chapter that they called "I Had a Good Teacher."
Les wrote, or said, probably said, and it was written down:
*It's still difficult for me to believe that Suzuki Roshi*
*accepted me so readily and completely as one of his disciples.
I now know that he is stemmed from his open and compassionate nature and his full acceptance of everyone.
However, like the other Los Altos students, I didn't see him very often.
And I felt very hesitant in approaching him or taking up any of his time.
He belonged to the San Francisco Zen Center, I thought.
We were lucky to get to see him once in a while.
When I did get to speak to him about being ordained, I went with a hesitant, cautious feeling.
We exchanged greetings and became silent.* This is him going up to San Francisco.
*He asked why I wanted to be ordained.
I gave him a reason, which wasn't very profound.
In fact, it was rather ordinary.* He doesn't say what the reason was.
*And then without a word, Suzuki Roshi stood up, went in the other room, and came back with Okasan, his wife, Mrs.
Suzuki, and a tape measure.
And immediately they began measuring me for robes.
So I let them turn me and tape me.
I held my arms out.
I listened to them discussing the final details of tailoring for the next hour.
Probably all in Japanese.
And I left in a daze, unsure when my ordination would take place, what I needed to do, or what I needed to learn to be a priest.
Only that it would take a few months for the robes to arrive from Japan.*
*Suzuki Roshi was usually at the center of things, but he did not need many words to understand a situation or to guide us.
He would take it in instantly, observing it quietly.
He had a great kindness and never hesitated to go somewhere or do something when requested.
And he had that wisdom to say the words or do the thing necessary at that moment.
As an example, I remember how I handled a particularly anxious moment at my ordination in December 1971.
The ceremony had begun and we were crowded together in the Los Altos Zendo when my mother arrived late.
I'll never forget Roshi's look, glancing at her as she entered and took a seat near the end of the platform, clearly anxious and upset about this strange unorthodox step that her son was taking.
Roshi went over to her,* like interrupting the ceremony, *went over to her very gently, reached over, put a hand on her shoulder and said, "You came at the right time."
And so I became one of his disciples.
But I didn't visit San Francisco Zen Center to see him very often, again for that fear of disturbing him or taking up his valuable time.
I did make it a point to see him at least once every three months.
I didn't want to run to him with all my problems, but I did want to see him occasionally.
So I told him whatever was greatest concern to me at the time.* And later he realized he probably could have gone every week if he wanted to.
So you're a human, perfectly happy either way.
We do make up these rules in our heads.
And the other thing, of course, Les didn't know in January of 1971 was that in December of that same year, Suzuki Roshi would pass away.
He was only with his teacher, an hour away from his teacher, for a little less than a year.
Suzuki Roshi made that kind of impression on people.
All the disciples have stories like this.
Personally, I do think for sure from all the stories I've read, of course, I never met him either, that he was indeed quite intuitive and quite skillful.
Although sometimes I wonder if some of his quietness was just that he didn't really trust his English that much.
That could have been true too.
Sometimes there's this sort of Orientalism, the inscrutable Asian teacher.
Sometimes it's because they're not really quite sure what to say, so they keep quiet.
And the other reason I suspect this, this is just me saying with full respect and love for all involved: Japanese has very intricate rules of politeness.
You have to say things the right way to not be rude, like even different verb conjugations, depending on your relative ranking of you and the other person and stuff like that.
And so I wonder if that made Suzuki Roshi say, "I don't know how to say it right here in America, so I'll just say just a few words.
It's probably better.
Probably better."
And it was better for them.

Another thing I learned from Les K that I now am doing once a year, if that seems about right, that I'm pretty certain I never asked anybody this, but I'm pretty certain he got this also from Suzuki Roshi, was at the end of zazen, at Kannon Do, at the Zendo, there in Mountain View.
Les wouldn't just leave as the officiating priest.
He'd stand at the doorway, right in the doors over here.
He'd stand next to the door in gassho, waiting.
And people would come up to him one at a time and he would bow with you.
Maybe in a way he was reenacting that moment at lunch so many years before.
Just that bow was enough.
His first real greeting of Suzuki Roshi, his teacher.
So every time I went, I got that moment of bowing, one on one with Les, like everyone else did.
And I really appreciated it.
That was a very beautiful moment, but also something that we don't do regularly because it would be easy to misunderstand what's that about.
So I thought of doing that at the opening ceremony for the temple, bowing with each person.
And then we did a similar ceremony a year later.
So that will be our custom here, maybe.
The abbot will bow to all of us at least once a year.
We bow to each other all the time.
Let me read one of his essays where he's actually talking to us about his understanding of practice, and then we'll come towards a close.
This is what they put in the first chapter, the first position of the book entitled *You Have to Get Wet*.
*If someone asks you what is Zen, you might want to share some teachings you've heard or talk about the history of Buddhism, or tell them about your practice.
Or you might simply say, "Zen cannot be explained."*
Yaoshan Weiyan, from the eighth century, from China now, was asked to give a lecture at his monastery.
*So he walked up to the large chair at the front of the hall where he would sit when giving Dharma talks.
And then without saying a word, he turned around and went straight back to his room.
Later, his attendant asked him, "Why didn't you speak?"
Yaoshan replied, "There is no need to say anything."
And he added, "If you want to study intellectually, you can go to a philosopher.
I don't need to speak.
I just practice with you."
This statement conveys the spirit of thousands of Zen masters who have dedicated their lives to their students and the practice.*
You can see why Les would pick that as a favorite story.
And by the way, none of these chapters are quite short, and I think probably his talks were quite short.
He goes on.
*Answering what is Zen is like answering what is the ocean.
To really understand the ocean, you have to submerge yourself.
You have to get wet.
You can dive into the first wave or bend your knees and let the wave wash over you, or if your timing is right, you can walk in without being knocked over.
But it's only after immersing yourself and engaging with the water that you know what it means to be wet.
You can't just talk about what wetness is.
You have to experience it.
If you stand at the water's edge and dip your toe in, you won't really know the ocean.
In Zen, we listen with our whole body, with our hopes, and with an empty mind.
Without trying to comprehend what it is intellectually and figure it out, without making a big deal about what we're doing.
This is the way of immersion in Zen.*
*There are thousands of academic studies on Zen, so many you probably wouldn't be able to read them all if you devoted your whole life to it.
Some are thoughtful, some profound, some share stories from deep within the history of Buddhism.
Studying these can be a help for us to understand the mind and the feelings and the world views of Buddhists and scholars over the centuries.
Explanations and studies can open the door and give us a glimpse, but we can't really understand the practice this way.
As a subject of study, Zen can be something we talk about or write about, but ultimately we can't really talk about it.
We can only experience it.
Viscerally, intuitively, in a feeling way.
We understand practice in our gut, not in our head.*
*There's another Zen story from the Blue Cliff Record collection of stories.
The story is about the fourth patriarch of Chinese Zen, Daoxin, sixth century now, who had three attendants, Guishan, Yunzhu, and Guo An.
Daoxin, the teacher, asked Guishan, one of the students, "With mouth and lips closed, how would you say it?"* Great Zen question.
*Guishan replied, "I would ask you to say it."* It's italicized with an exclamation mark, so maybe less shouted out.
*I would ask you to say it.
And Daoxin, the teacher, told him, "I could.
If I did, I'd have no successors."* I'd have no successors, meaning it would just confuse things.
It wouldn't be the real thing.
*This teacher's question means, how do you express truth?
How do you express truth in everyday actions?
His disciple Guishan says he can respond only if he doesn't use his intellect.
Daoxin, the teacher, replies that if he were to speak, he wouldn't have successors, affirming a student's response that he shouldn't rely on intellect either.
Zen practice and life have to be understood through experience, like going into the ocean to understand Zen practice and our life.
We need confidence and dedication.
When we're confused, which is a lot of the time, we have to work to unravel the confusion.
So we keep practicing.
Time is not a consideration.
Practice without end is our attitude.
And it's that kind of confidence that awakens our insight, our understanding.*
So that's pretty good, huh?
Don't try to figure it out.

And one of the things that's, I think, so wonderful for us about having this meditation practice, this zazen practice, at the center of all this, is we have these fabulous and sustained opportunities to watch our busy minds doing all the things that he's telling us won't help.
Watch our minds racing and figuring and comparing and judging and doubting and worrying and fretting.
And simple instructions are usually given, right?
Like, oh, go back to your breath.
What a relief if you can just for one moment just be present and breathe.
But pretty soon it's all back, and you realize that trying to follow the instructions very carefully is not going to solve this exactly.
But as he says, there's no hurry.
We're patient.
We practice this way for our whole life.
And my theory about how zazen actually works and how awakening works is eventually, and it may take many decades, you just get tired of all that, and you give it up.
One day you notice, oh, I'm not doing that so much.
I'm not doing so much judging and worrying and figuring and comparing and analyzing and intellectualizing.
So I think Les K is a wonderful model, a wonderful example for so many of this side of it, just the steadiness, the patience, the willingness.
Like he says, we're confused most of the time, but he doesn't say in there that's a bad thing.
And I think what he means is it's fine to be confused.
It's a necessary condition for awakening to be confused, but stick around, stay with it.
Confusion will get thinner, maybe like mist or clouds from time to time.
You'll see the sun and you won't jump up and run around and start telling everybody what the sun is, right, because they have to, what, experience it for themselves.
I didn't put Lester's picture up on the altar of the ancestors because we only have so much room.
I'm trying to just put people that we have some direct practice connection to as a teacher.
But he does make me think of Sojun Mel Weitsman, whose picture I also just put up.
I had very much the same approach.
He was the teacher at Berkeley Zen Center, which was a little bigger and, maybe more vital in some ways, a little more dynamic, maybe just maybe because of the people who happen to be in Berkeley.
I don't know.
But same thing.
These early disciples of Suzuki Roshi, which is our lineage, they varied a lot.
They were individuals, but a few of them were like Les K and like Sojun Mel Weitsman.
They somehow realized almost intuitively.
I don't know that Suzuki Roshi ever gave them any much specific sort of advice or anything like that.
Probably not.
But they somehow just felt in their bones and stuck with it and had enough faith and trust to stick with it year after year after year after year.
And it's pretty new still here in America, right?

So we had to be a little bit audacious to buy an $800,000 building and figure it all out, if we had a place where people sit around and do nothing and produce nothing, that that would be helpful and people would want to come and at least enough of them would want to support it, become members and give a donation or something.
But it would actually work out, you know, wouldn't just have to sell it back to the bank later.
I was imagining a meeting with the bank manager saying, "Oh, it didn't work out.
You have to sell it back."
"Oh, what was your business plan?"
"Nothing."
Now, hopefully we'll never have that meeting and still have that business plan.
Nothing.
Nothing.
They do it for a really long time.
And I think the other thing I think about here too is there are a lot of problems in the world.
We all know, especially the governmental and political news is so tangled and horrible, maybe worse than usual.
So are we actually helping by sitting here doing nothing?
I think so.
I think so.
Some people are called to be the counterweight, and we still get to have dynamic lives and get excited and have fun and go out and do things.
And I'm sure Les had fun with his family, traveled at least a little bit, enjoyed his life, but he was called to be the counterweight.
Be one of the ones who just sits down and is willing to sit down for everybody, not just for himself.
That's the other thing.
I was saying before you have to have lots of faith and trust, but I think that's really what enables the faith and trust.
If you're thinking I'm just doing this so that I'll feel better, I think you wouldn't be able to last a year, much less 50 years.
But if you start to feel, as I think Les deeply did in a quiet way, this is all of us sitting together for all of us.
I just have more influence over this one body, and I'm choosing to bring this body to the temple every morning until I can't anymore.
I do it for all of us.
And it's not even me, it's we, always.
Thank you, Les K for your life and your practice touching us here today.
Anyone have any thoughts or comments about all that before we go?
We have a couple of minutes.
Where does that feel like enough?
Funny asking people to comment on a hard talk, which is about no explanations.
We're good.
Okay.
Thanks for listening.
